title: Mixture Models and the EM Algorithm
description: Latent variables, Gaussian mixtures, the expectation–maximization algorithm, its derivation from Jensen's inequality and its practical use.
overview: Real data often come from several overlapping sources: heights of adults from two sexes, pixel colors from foreground and background, customer visits from several behavior types. If we knew which source produced each point, fitting would be easy: estimate each source separately. But the source label is hidden. Hidden variables like this are called latent variables, and they turn simple estimation into a harder problem.

The expectation–maximization (EM) algorithm solves it by alternating between guessing the hidden labels (softly) and re-estimating the parameters as if the guess were right. It is one of the most important algorithms in machine learning and is the basis of mixture models, hidden Markov models and many others.
objectives: Write a Gaussian mixture model as a latent variable model and compute responsibilities.
Run the E-step and M-step of EM for a Gaussian mixture by hand.
Derive EM from Jensen's inequality and the evidence lower bound, and show that it never decreases the likelihood.
Explain the relation between EM for Gaussian mixtures and k-means.
Handle practical issues: initialization, singularities, constrained covariances and choosing the number of components.

sections.title: Gaussian mixture models
body: A **mixture model** says that each data point x was generated in two steps: first a hidden label z ∈ {1, …, k} is drawn with probability φ_j = P(z = j), and then x is drawn from the distribution of component z. For a **Gaussian mixture model** (GMM) the components are Gaussians:

eq: p(x) = Σ_{j=1}^{k} φ_j N(x; μ_j, Σ_j)

body: The numbers φ_j are the **mixing proportions**. The variable z is **latent**: it is part of the model but never observed.

body.caption: A mixture of two Gaussians (dashed) and their weighted sum (solid).

body: Given a point, Bayes' rule gives the probability that it came from component j, the **responsibility**:
This is a **soft assignment**: a point between two components belongs partly to each. Compare the hard assignment of k-means.
The log-likelihood of the data is

body.eq: ℓ(φ, μ, Σ) = Σ_i ln Σ_j φ_j N(x^{(i)}; μ_j, Σ_j)

body: The sum inside the logarithm prevents a closed form: the derivative couples all the parameters. If the labels z were known, the likelihood would be Σ_i ln φ_{z_i} N(x^{(i)}; μ_{z_i}, Σ_{z_i}), and the maximum likelihood estimates would be the class frequencies, class means and class covariances of Gaussian discriminant analysis. EM uses this: it fills in the labels with their expected values.

check.q: In a Gaussian mixture, the responsibility w_{ij} is
check.a: the posterior probability that point i came from component j
wrong: the prior probability of component j
the distance from point i to the mean of component j
the number of points in component j

sections.title: EM for Gaussian mixtures
body: EM breaks a chicken-and-egg problem. If we knew which component produced each point, we could estimate each component's mean and spread by simple averaging. If we knew each component's mean and spread, we could work out how likely each component is to have produced each point. We know neither, so we start with a guess for one and alternate: use the guessed parameters to estimate the memberships, then use the memberships to improve the parameters. Each round is a little better than the last.
Starting from initial parameters, repeat two steps until convergence.

list: **E-step**: with the current parameters, compute the responsibilities w_{ij} for every point and component.
**M-step**: re-estimate the parameters as weighted maximum likelihood, with weights w_{ij}.

eq: μ_j = Σ_i w_{ij} x^{(i)} / Σ_i w_{ij}
Σ_j = Σ_i w_{ij} (x^{(i)} − μ_j)(x^{(i)} − μ_j)ᵀ / Σ_i w_{ij}

body: Each formula is the usual one (frequency, mean, covariance) with every point counted w_{ij} times for component j.

example.title: One EM iteration
example.problem: Data x = 1, 3, 5, 7. Two components with known unit variance and equal weights 0.5, and current means μ₁ = 2, μ₂ = 6. Do one E-step and update the means.
solution: With unit variances and equal weights, w_{i1} ∝ exp(−(x_i − 2)²/2) and w_{i2} ∝ exp(−(x_i − 6)²/2).
The points 3 and 5 are the ambiguous ones. Weights for component 1 sum to 1 + 0.982 + 0.018 = 2.000, and the weighted sum of x is 1 + 2.946 + 0.090 = 4.036, so μ₁ = 2.018. By symmetry μ₂ = 5.982.
Each mean moved a little toward the ambiguous middle points. Repeating the iteration, the means converge near 2 and 6, which match the two obvious groups of points {1, 3} and {5, 7}.

body: Suppose all components share a spherical covariance σ²I and equal weights. As σ → 0, the responsibilities become exactly 0 or 1 (each point belongs to the nearest mean), and the M-step becomes the centroid update. So k-means is the hard-assignment limit of EM for a Gaussian mixture. In return, EM can model clusters of different sizes, shapes and orientations through the covariances Σ_j.

A fitted GMM is a generative model. To sample, draw z from φ, then draw x from N(μ_z, Σ_z). It can also detect outliers (points of low p(x)) and, by using the conditional distribution given some features, fill in missing values.

sections.title: Why EM works: the evidence lower bound
body: The intuition for why the two steps work: the true log-likelihood is hard to maximize directly because of the sum inside the logarithm. EM builds an easier function that always lies below it and touches it at the current parameters, climbs to the top of that easier function, and then builds a new one at the new point. Each climb moves the true likelihood up as well, since the easier function never exceeds it. The details follow.

For a general latent variable model p(x, z; θ) with observed x and hidden z, we want to maximize the log-likelihood of the data, ℓ(θ) = Σ_i ln Σ_z p(x^{(i)}, z; θ). EM maximizes it by repeatedly maximizing a lower bound.
For a concave function such as the logarithm, the log of an average is at least the average of the logs: ln E[X] ≥ E[ln X], with equality when X is constant.
For one example, introduce any distribution Q(z) over the latent variable. Then

eq: ln p(x; θ) = ln Σ_z Q(z) · p(x, z; θ)/Q(z)
≥ Σ_z Q(z) ln ( p(x, z; θ)/Q(z) )  =: ELBO(Q, θ)

body: This is the **evidence lower bound** (ELBO), by Jensen's inequality with the average taken over z ~ Q. The bound is tight when p(x, z; θ)/Q(z) is the same for all z, which happens exactly when Q is the posterior, Q(z) = p(z | x; θ). EM alternates:

list: **E-step**: set Q_i(z) = p(z | x^{(i)}; θ_t). This makes the bound tight at the current θ: ELBO(Q, θ_t) = ℓ(θ_t). For a GMM this Q is the responsibilities.

**M-step**: maximize the bound over θ with Q fixed: θ_{t+1} = argmax_θ Σ_i Σ_z Q_i(z) ln p(x^{(i)}, z; θ). This is the expected complete-data log-likelihood, which has the 'weighted maximum likelihood' form that is easy to maximize.

body.key: EM never decreases the likelihood: ℓ(θ_{t+1}) ≥ ELBO(Q_t, θ_{t+1}) ≥ ELBO(Q_t, θ_t) = ℓ(θ_t). The first inequality is the bound, the second is the M-step, and the equality is the tight E-step. The likelihood is bounded above, so the sequence converges. The limit is a local maximum (or saddle point), not necessarily the global one.

body.note: The same bound is the objective of variational inference. When the exact posterior is too hard to compute, one restricts Q to a simple family and maximizes the ELBO over both Q and θ. Variational autoencoders (see Generative Models) are built on this idea.

check.a: the posterior p(z | x; θ) under the current parameters

a uniform distribution

check.q: Which statement about EM is true?
check.a: The log-likelihood is non-decreasing across iterations
wrong: It always finds the global maximum
It requires labeled data
It works only for Gaussian components

list: **Initialization.** EM finds a local maximum, so start from several initializations, often from the output of k-means, and keep the run with the highest likelihood.

**Singularities.** The likelihood is unbounded: a component centered on a single data point with variance σ² → 0 gives density → ∞. Guard against it with a small ridge added to each covariance (Σ_j + εI), a prior on the covariances, or a minimum number of points per component.
**Constrained covariances.** A full covariance has n(n + 1)/2 parameters per component. Use a diagonal (axis-aligned), spherical (σ²I) or tied (shared) covariance when n is large relative to m.

**Number of components.** The likelihood always rises with k, so use a penalized criterion. The **Bayesian information criterion** BIC = −2 ln L + p ln m, with p the number of free parameters, balances fit against complexity. Choose k with the lowest BIC, or use a held-out likelihood.
**Speed.** Each iteration costs O(mkn²) for full covariances. Convergence can be slow, and is often declared when the log-likelihood changes by less than a tolerance.

example.title: Counting parameters for BIC
example.problem: A 3-component GMM with full covariances is fit to data with n = 2 features. How many free parameters does it have?
example.solution: Means: 3 × 2 = 6. Covariances: 3 × (2·3/2) = 9. Mixing proportions: k − 1 = 2 (they sum to one). Total p = 17.

list: **Missing data.** Treat the missing values as latent variables.
**Hidden Markov models**: the Baum–Welch algorithm is EM, with the hidden states as latent variables (see Graphical Models).
**Topic models** (such as latent Dirichlet allocation) with latent topic assignments, **factor analysis** and **probabilistic PCA** (see PCA and Dimensionality Reduction).
**Semi-supervised learning**: labels for some points are observed, and for the rest are latent.

check.q: Why does an unconstrained Gaussian mixture likelihood have degenerate solutions?
check.a: A component centered on one point can shrink its variance to zero and make the density, hence the likelihood, arbitrarily large
wrong: The mixing proportions can be negative
The responsibilities do not sum to one
EM always diverges

quiz.q: How is one new data point sampled from a fitted Gaussian mixture?
quiz.a: Draw a component z with probability φ_z, then draw x from N(μ_z, Σ_z)
wrong: Draw x from every component and average the draws, weighted by φ
Draw x from a single Gaussian whose mean is Σ_j φ_j μ_j
Compute the responsibilities of a random point and keep the most likely component's mean
quiz.why: The model is a two-step process: a hidden label first, then an observation from that label's Gaussian. Averaging draws would produce a single blurred point rather than a sample from the mixture.

quiz.q: A two-component mixture has φ = (0.25, 0.75). At a point x, the component densities are N(x; μ₁, Σ₁) = 0.4 and N(x; μ₂, Σ₂) = 0.1. The responsibility of component 1 is
quiz.why: The weighted densities are 0.25 × 0.4 = 0.10 and 0.75 × 0.1 = 0.075, so w₁ = 0.10/0.175 = 4/7. The value 0.8 = 0.4/0.5 ignores the mixing proportions, and 3/7 is the responsibility of component 2.

quiz.q: Four points x = 1, 2, 6, 8 have responsibilities for component 1 of 0.9, 0.7, 0.2, 0.2. After the M-step, what is μ₁?
quiz.why: The weighted sum is 0.9 + 1.4 + 1.2 + 1.6 = 5.1 and the weights sum to 2.0, so μ₁ = 2.55. The value 4.25 is the unweighted mean, 5.1 forgets to normalize, and 1.275 divides by m.

quiz.q: Why does maximum likelihood for a Gaussian mixture have no closed-form solution?
quiz.a: The sum over components sits inside the logarithm, so the derivative couples all the parameters
wrong: Gaussian densities are not differentiable in their covariance matrices, which blocks the usual calculus derivation of the estimates
The mixing proportions must sum to one, which rules out calculus
The latent labels are continuous, so the sum cannot be evaluated
quiz.why: ln Σ_j φ_j N(x; μ_j, Σ_j) does not split into separate terms per component. With known labels the log would apply to a single term and the estimates would be simple frequencies, means and covariances.

quiz.q: How does EM deal with the component labels that are not observed?
quiz.a: It uses the posterior probabilities of the labels, computed under the current parameters, as weights
wrong: It discards points whose labels are unknown
It sets each label to the single most likely component and then fits
It samples each label once from the mixing proportions φ and keeps those sampled labels fixed for the whole run
quiz.why: Filling in the labels with their expected values (the responsibilities) gives weighted maximum likelihood. Setting each label to its most likely value is the hard-assignment limit that gives k-means.

quiz.q: Which quantities are held fixed while the M-step updates the parameters of a Gaussian mixture?
quiz.a: The responsibilities computed in the preceding E-step
wrong: The means μ_j, which are re-estimated only in the E-step
The covariances Σ_j, which are estimated once at initialization
The mixing proportions φ_j, which are set by the user
quiz.why: The M-step treats the responsibilities as given weights and re-estimates φ, μ and Σ from them. The E-step is the one that uses the old parameters to recompute the responsibilities.

quiz.q: Two overlapping clusters are elongated ellipses tilted at different angles. Why can a Gaussian mixture with full covariances describe them better than k-means?
quiz.a: Each component has its own covariance, so it can take its own size, shape and orientation
wrong: EM minimizes squared distance more accurately than Lloyd's algorithm does
A mixture does not need the number of components to be chosen
EM is guaranteed to reach the global optimum, which k-means is not
quiz.why: k-means uses Euclidean distance to a mean and so favors round clusters of similar size. The covariances Σ_j in a GMM give each cluster a different shape, and soft assignment handles the overlap.

quiz.q: A GMM has been fit to data. Which point is flagged as an outlier?
quiz.a: One where the mixture density p(x) is very low
wrong: One whose responsibilities are spread almost evenly between two components
One whose largest responsibility is exactly 1
One with the highest value of φ_j for its component
quiz.why: A fitted mixture is a density model, so a point of very low p(x) is unlikely under every component. Even responsibilities mark a point between two components, which can be perfectly typical.

quiz.q: X equals 2 or 8, each with probability 1/2. Which pair gives ln E[X] and E[ln X]?
quiz.why: E[X] = 5 so ln E[X] = ln 5 = 1.609. E[ln X] = (ln 2 + ln 8)/2 = ln 4 = 1.386. Jensen's inequality for the concave log gives ln E[X] ≥ E[ln X], with equality only if X is constant.

quiz.q: In the chain ℓ(θ_{t+1}) ≥ ELBO(Q_t, θ_{t+1}) ≥ ELBO(Q_t, θ_t) = ℓ(θ_t), the second inequality holds because
quiz.a: the M-step chose θ_{t+1} to maximize the bound for the fixed Q_t
wrong: Jensen's inequality applies to the logarithm
the E-step set Q to the posterior, which made the bound equal to the likelihood at the current parameters θ_t
the likelihood of a mixture is concave in θ
quiz.why: The first inequality is the bound itself (Jensen), the equality is the tight bound from the E-step, and the middle step is the M-step improving the bound. Nothing here requires the likelihood to be concave.

quiz.q: The M-step of EM maximizes, over θ with Q held fixed,
quiz.a: the expected complete-data log-likelihood Σ_i Σ_z Q_i(z) ln p(x^{(i)}, z; θ)
wrong: the observed-data log-likelihood Σ_i ln p(x^{(i)}; θ) directly
the entropy of Q
the distance between Q and the posterior
quiz.why: With Q fixed, the entropy term of the ELBO does not depend on θ. What remains is a weighted complete-data log-likelihood, which has a simple closed-form maximizer for a mixture of Gaussians.

quiz.q: Two EM runs from different initializations end with log-likelihoods of −510 and −498. What is the right conclusion?
quiz.a: Keep the run at −498; both are only local maxima, so neither is known to be the global one
wrong: Average the two sets of parameters, since both converged
The run at −510 must have failed to converge, because EM run to convergence always reaches the global maximum
The run at −498 is the global maximum because it is higher
quiz.why: EM never decreases the likelihood but stops at a local maximum or saddle point, so different starts can give different answers. The higher likelihood is the better model found, yet there is no certificate that it is the best possible.

quiz.q: One component of a fitted GMM has a covariance near zero around a single data point, and the log-likelihood is enormous. What is the standard remedy?
quiz.a: Add a small ridge εI to each covariance, or require a minimum number of points per component
wrong: Run more EM iterations until the covariance recovers
Increase the number of components
Drop the mixing proportions and use equal weights
quiz.why: A component centered on one point with variance shrinking to zero makes the density, hence the likelihood, grow without bound. The ridge keeps covariances from collapsing. More iterations only push further into the singularity.

quiz.q: A full-covariance GMM has k = 3 components on n = 100 features. How many free covariance parameters does it have?
quiz.why: Each symmetric covariance has n(n + 1)/2 = 5,050 parameters, so three components have 15,150. The value 30,000 ignores symmetry, and 300 counts only the diagonals.

quiz.q: Two GMMs are fit to m = 100 points. Model A has ln L = −300 with 5 free parameters. Model B has ln L = −290 with 17. Using BIC = −2 ln L + p ln m (ln 100 ≈ 4.605), which is preferred?
quiz.a: A, because its BIC of about 623 is below B's of about 658
wrong: B, because its log-likelihood is higher and the extra parameters were needed to reach that fit
B, because its BIC of about 658 is above A's of about 623
Neither, since BIC cannot compare models with different numbers of parameters
quiz.why: BIC = 600 + 23.0 for A and 580 + 78.3 for B, and the lowest BIC wins. The penalty of 12 extra parameters outweighs the gain of 10 in log-likelihood.

quiz.q: The Baum–Welch algorithm for fitting a hidden Markov model is
quiz.a: EM, with the hidden states playing the role of the latent variables
wrong: k-means run on the sequence of observations
gradient descent on the labels of the states
EM, but with the observations treated as latent
quiz.why: In an HMM the states are never observed, which is exactly the latent variable setting: the E-step computes state posteriors and the M-step re-estimates the transition and emission parameters.

summary: A mixture model draws a hidden label z, then x from component z. For a GMM, p(x) = Σ φ_j N(x; μ_j, Σ_j), and the responsibility w_{ij} is the posterior of component j for point i.
The log-likelihood has a sum inside the log, so there is no closed form. EM alternates an E-step (compute responsibilities) and an M-step (weighted frequencies, means and covariances).
EM maximizes the evidence lower bound. The E-step sets Q to the posterior, making the bound tight. The M-step maximizes the bound. The likelihood never decreases, but EM finds only a local maximum.
k-means is the hard-assignment, σ → 0 limit of EM for a spherical Gaussian mixture.
Initialize with k-means and restart, protect against singular covariances, constrain covariances in high dimension, and choose k by BIC or held-out likelihood.

problems.q: A two-component 1D mixture has φ = (0.5, 0.5), means 0 and 4 and unit variances. Compute the responsibility of component 2 for x = 3.
problems.solution: Component 1 density ∝ exp(−9/2) = 0.01111; component 2 ∝ exp(−1/2) = 0.6065 (the common 1/√(2π) and the equal weights cancel). w₂ = 0.6065/(0.6065 + 0.0111) = 0.982.

problems.q: A mixture has φ = (0.3, 0.7) and for a point x the component densities are N₁ = 0.2 and N₂ = 0.05. Find the point's responsibilities and the contribution of this point to the log-likelihood.
problems.solution: Weighted: 0.3(0.2) = 0.06 and 0.7(0.05) = 0.035. The sum is 0.095. Responsibilities (0.631, 0.368). The contribution to ℓ is ln 0.095 = −2.354.

problems.q: Starting from the example in the text (x = 1, 3, 5, 7; means 2 and 6), what would the new weights φ be after the first M-step?
problems.solution: φ₁ = (Σ_i w_{i1})/m = 2.000/4 = 0.5, and φ₂ = 0.5. By symmetry the weights do not change.

problems.q: A GMM with k = 4 components, full covariances, and n = 3 features. Count the free parameters.
Use Jensen's inequality to show that ln(0.5 · 1 + 0.5 · 9) ≥ 0.5 ln 1 + 0.5 ln 9.
problems.solution: Left side: ln 5 = 1.609. Right side: 0.5(0) + 0.5(2.197) = 1.099. Indeed 1.609 ≥ 1.099, with a gap because the values 1 and 9 differ.
